blocks.body: Losing job-based coverage opens two clocks. COBRA lets you keep the same employer plan, generally for up to 18 months after a job loss, and you have at least 60 days to elect it; an election made in that window covers you back to the day job coverage ended, and you owe the premiums for that time. The premium can be up to 102% of the full cost, because the employer subsidy ends. Losing coverage is also a qualifying event for a Marketplace special enrollment period that runs from 60 days before to 60 days after the loss, where premium tax credits are based on your expected income for the year, which may now be lower. Count severance, unemployment pay, any 401(k) withdrawal and wages from a new job in that estimate, and report income changes as they happen: starting with 2026, advance credits above what you qualify for must be repaid in full, and household income above 400% of the poverty line generally gets no federal credit. Medicaid, and CHIP for children, accept applications any time of year and judge eligibility on current monthly income. A spouse's employer plan must offer at least a 30-day special enrollment window. Choosing COBRA and later dropping it, or stopping payment, does not reopen the Marketplace: once 60 days have passed since job coverage ended, you generally must wait for open enrollment unless COBRA runs out, an employer subsidy for it ends, or you have another life event. Before coverage ends, use any health FSA balance on care you need, since the full year's election is available to spend; an HSA can pay COBRA premiums, and health premiums while you receive unemployment, tax-free. Compare every option on total cost, not premium alone.
blocks.plain: When job-based health coverage ends, two clocks start. COBRA lets you stay on the same employer plan, generally for up to 18 months after a job loss. You get at least 60 days to sign up. If you sign up in that time, coverage reaches back to the day your job coverage ended, and you pay the premiums for that time. It can cost up to 102% of the full premium, because your employer stops paying its share. Losing coverage also lets you sign up on the Marketplace from 60 days before to 60 days after the coverage ends. There, help with premiums is based on what you expect to earn this year, which may now be less. Count severance, unemployment pay, any 401(k) money you take out and pay from a new job. Tell the Marketplace about income changes right away. Starting with 2026, if you got more help than you qualify for, you must pay all of it back at tax time, and household income above 400% of the poverty line generally gets no federal help. Medicaid, and CHIP for children, take applications any time of year and look at what you earn each month now. If your spouse has a job-based plan, it must give you at least 30 days to join. If you choose COBRA and later drop it or stop paying, the Marketplace does not open again for you: once 60 days have passed since your job coverage ended, you usually have to wait for open enrollment, unless COBRA runs out, your old employer stops paying part of it, or you have another life event. Before your coverage ends, use any money in a health FSA on care you need, because the whole year's amount is there to spend. An HSA can pay COBRA premiums, and health premiums while you get unemployment, without tax. Compare every option by total cost, not just the monthly premium.

blocks.body: Add expected after-tax severance and unemployment pay to liquid savings, then divide by essential monthly spending to get months of runway. Unemployment insurance is run by your state, so file with the state agency as soon as you are out of work, even if you are not sure you qualify; the state, not your employer, decides. Pay reported on a 1099 generally does not count toward a regular claim, and many states hold back or reduce benefits for the weeks severance covers. Benefits are taxable federal income, so consider voluntary withholding. Severance is taxable wages and is normally paid with withholding. If cash is tight, cover housing, utilities, food, insurance, the transportation that keeps you working and any court-ordered payments such as child support first, then keep at least the minimum payment on every debt current; call lenders about hardship plans before a payment is missed. For federal student loans, ask your servicer about an income-driven plan, where the payment can be as low as $0 in some cases, or an unemployment deferment, and keep paying until a deferment is granted. If savings will not cover a month, apply for SNAP food benefits through your state now, because benefits count from the date you apply.
blocks.plain: Add the severance (after tax) and unemployment pay you expect to your cash savings. Then divide by what you must spend each month. That is how many months you can last. Unemployment pay is run by your state, so apply with your state as soon as you are out of work, even if you are not sure you qualify. The state decides, not your employer. Pay reported on a 1099 form usually does not count toward a regular claim, and many states hold back or cut benefits for the weeks your severance covers. Unemployment pay counts as income for federal tax, so think about having tax taken out. Severance is taxed like pay and usually has tax taken out already. If money is tight, pay for housing, utilities, food, insurance, the transportation that gets you to work and any payments a court has ordered, such as child support, first. Then keep at least the minimum payment on every debt current, and call your lenders about hardship plans before you miss a payment. For federal student loans, ask your loan servicer about an income-driven plan, where the payment can be as low as $0 in some cases, or an unemployment deferment. Keep paying until a deferment is approved. If your savings will not last a month, apply for SNAP food help through your state now, because benefits count from the day you apply.

blocks.body: The usual options are to leave it in the old plan, roll it to a new employer's plan, or roll it to an IRA. Cashing out triggers income tax, plus a 10% additional tax before age 59½ unless an exception applies, and a check paid to you carries 20% mandatory withholding; a direct trustee-to-trustee rollover avoids both. If a check has already been paid to you, you can still roll it over within 60 days, but you must make up the withheld 20% from other money or that part is taxed. If your balance is small, the plan can pay it out without your consent; unless you choose otherwise, it generally goes into an IRA opened in your name, though the smallest balances can arrive as a check, so watch your mail. If you truly need some of the money, withdraw only what you need and roll over the rest. If you separated from service in or after the year you turn 55, that plan (not an IRA) can pay out without the 10% additional tax, which argues for leaving it in place if you may need it. If the plan holds your employer's stock, check net unrealized appreciation before rolling it, because rolling the shares into an IRA gives up that treatment. If you have an outstanding 401(k) loan, find out when it comes due: an unpaid balance is treated as a distribution (taxable, plus the 10% additional tax before 59½), though a plan-loan offset within 12 months after leaving the job can still be rolled over until your tax-filing deadline, including extensions, for that year. If you make backdoor Roth contributions, a pre-tax IRA balance makes later conversions partly taxable, because all your traditional IRAs are counted together; keeping the money in a workplace plan, old or new, avoids that. Be cautious if anyone suggests moving the money into an annuity, and ask how they are paid.
blocks.plain: For the old job's retirement plan, the usual choices are: leave it in the old plan, move it to your new job's plan, or move it to an IRA. Cashing it out means income tax, plus an extra 10% tax before age 59½ unless an exception applies. A check made out to you also has 20% held back for tax. Moving the money straight from one account to the other (a direct rollover) avoids both. If a check was already sent to you, you can still move it into a retirement account within 60 days. But you must add back the 20% that was held back, using other money, or that part gets taxed. If your balance is small, the plan can pay it out without asking you. Unless you choose something else, it generally goes into an IRA opened in your name, but the smallest balances can come as a check, so watch your mail. If you really need some of the money, take out only what you need and move the rest. If you left the job in or after the year you turn 55, that plan — not an IRA — can pay you without the extra 10% tax. That is a reason to leave it where it is if you might need it. If the plan holds your employer's stock, look into net unrealized appreciation before moving it, because putting those shares into an IRA loses that tax treatment. If you still owe on a 401(k) loan, find out when it comes due: an unpaid balance counts as a withdrawal (taxed, plus the extra 10% tax before 59½), but if the plan takes the loan out of your balance within 12 months after you leave, you can still roll that amount over until your tax-filing deadline, including extensions, for that year. If you put money into a Roth IRA through the backdoor method, having pre-tax money in an IRA makes later conversions partly taxed, because all your traditional IRAs are counted together. Keeping the money in a job's plan, old or new, avoids that. Be careful if anyone suggests putting the money into an annuity, and ask how they get paid.

Backdoor Roth: a pre-tax IRA balance makes later conversions partly taxable because traditional IRAs are aggregated; keeping the money in a workplace plan (old or new) avoids that
all your traditional iras are counted together
Be cautious about an annuity pitch for the money; ask how the person is paid
The offset must occur within 12 months after leaving the job

Forced cash-out thresholds ($7,000 consent limit, $1,000 default-IRA line; read in 26 U.S.C. 411(a)(11) and 401(a)(31)(B)) are left out of the text on purpose, so no figure keys are needed. If the owner wants it shorter, the backdoor-Roth sentence (CFP-7) is the most specialized addition. ADV-8(a) title softening is drafted under owner_decisions. Reconciled 2026-11-16 with the factual corrections on branch fix/verification-2026-11-16.

blocks.body: Vested stock options often expire a fixed period after you leave, and incentive stock options lose their favorable treatment if not exercised within three months of termination of employment. The exact window is in your grant agreement; read it before it closes. Exercising takes cash and can create a tax bill: the gain on a nonqualified option is generally taxed as income when you exercise, and incentive stock options can trigger the alternative minimum tax. Weigh that against your runway before spending your emergency cushion to beat a deadline. Also check what your plan documents say about unvested RSUs, ESPP purchases and any deferred compensation.
blocks.plain: Stock options that have vested often expire a set time after you leave. Incentive stock options lose their special tax treatment if you don't exercise them within three months after your job ends. Your grant agreement has the exact deadline — read it before it passes. Buying the shares costs cash and can mean a tax bill. With a nonqualified option, the gain is usually taxed as income when you buy. Incentive stock options can set off the alternative minimum tax. Think about how long your money has to last before you use your emergency savings to beat a deadline. Also check what your plan papers say about RSUs that have not vested, ESPP purchases and any deferred pay.

blocks.body: A year with a gap, severance and two employers is the classic under- or over-withholding year. Run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator and file a new Form W-4 with the new employer. Each employer's payroll tracks the 401(k) limit separately, but the employee deferral limit ({{fig:limit_401k_deferral}} for 2026) is yours across all plans, so total both years' contributions yourself. If your total went over the limit, tell one plan early in the next year so it can return the excess by April 15; otherwise it is taxed twice. Extra Social Security tax withheld because you had two employers generally comes back as a credit on your tax return.
blocks.plain: A year with a gap, severance and two employers often ends with too much or too little tax taken out. Use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator and give your new employer a new Form W-4. Each employer's payroll only tracks its own 401(k). But the yearly limit on what you put in ({{fig:limit_401k_deferral}} for 2026) is yours across all plans, so add up both jobs' contributions yourself. If you put in too much in total, tell one plan early in the next year so it can give back the extra by April 15. If not, that money is taxed twice. If two employers together took out too much Social Security tax, you can generally get it back as a credit on your tax return.

April 15 is from 26 U.S.C. 402(g)(2)(A)(ii); the March 1 allocation step in (A)(i) is carried as 'early in the next year' so no new number enters; the IRS consequences page says 'by the due date of your tax return', the same date in an ordinary year. Note 'Form W-4' and '401(k)' put 4 and 401 in the number set; both are unchanged in body and plain.

new_claims.claim: A COBRA election made during the election period gives coverage from the date coverage would otherwise have been lost, and the plan may charge the premium for that period (first payment not due before 45 days after the election)
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 26 CFR 54.4980B-6 Q&A-3(a) ('If the election is made during that period, coverage must be provided from the date that coverage would otherwise have been lost'), read on eCFR as of 2026-11-12; 29 U.S.C. 1162(3) (premium for any period of continuation coverage; no premium required before 45 days after the initial election), govinfo. Added 2026-11-16 from the §4.4 persona pass (CFP-1).

new_claims.claim: For loss of minimum essential coverage, the Marketplace special enrollment window runs from 60 days before to 60 days after the loss
new_claims.source: 45 CFR 155.420(c)(2), (d)(1)(i); DOL EBSA 'An Employee's Guide to Health Benefits Under COBRA'
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 45 CFR 155.420(c)(2) (60 days before and, unless the (c)(6) Medicaid/CHIP option applies, 60 days after the triggering event, for individuals in (d)(1)), read on eCFR as of 2026-11-12; the DOL COBRA guide (Sept. 2022, read via a fetch tool) says 'within 60 days before or after losing your job-based coverage'. Narrows CL484 for the job-loss block only. Added from the persona pass (CFP-65).

new_claims.claim: Voluntarily dropping COBRA, or stopping premium payments before it runs out, is not a loss of coverage for a Marketplace special enrollment period; outside open enrollment a switch is allowed within 60 days of losing job-based coverage, when COBRA runs out, when the former employer stops contributing to COBRA, or after another qualifying life event
new_claims.source: 45 CFR 155.420(e)(1); HealthCare.gov 'COBRA coverage when you're unemployed'; DOL EBSA COBRA guide
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 45 CFR 155.420(e) ('Loss of coverage does not include voluntary termination of coverage or other loss due to ... failure to pay premiums ... including COBRA continuation coverage premiums prior to expiration'); HealthCare.gov lists the outside-open-enrollment switches (COBRA running out; employer contribution ends; 'still within 60 days of when you lost your job-based coverage'); the DOL guide: terminating COBRA early with no other event means waiting for open enrollment. The employer-subsidy-ends exception (155.420(e)(1), (d)(15)) is now in the block text. Checker 2026-11-16: 'switch only at open enrollment or when COBRA runs out' corrected to include it and other life events. Added from the persona pass (ADV-5, CFP-1).

new_claims.claim: The Marketplace income estimate counts wages, unemployment compensation and most 401(k) withdrawals; changes should be reported as they happen; for tax years after 2025 excess advance premium tax credit is repaid in full, and the federal credit is generally limited to household income of no more than 400% of the federal poverty line
new_claims.source: IRC §36B as amended by P.L. 119-21 (repayment limitation removed for tax years after 2025); IRS 'Questions and answers on the Premium Tax Credit' (Q7, Q31); IRS 'Repayment caps eliminated for excess advance payments of the Premium Tax Credit'; HealthCare.gov 'What to include as income'
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at IRS and HealthCare.gov pages: IRS Q&A Q7 (updated 2026-02-19: eligible if household income 'at least 100 percent but no more than 400 percent', with the 2021-2025 expansion now over) and the repayment-caps page ('Beginning with tax year 2026, the taxpayer must repay the full amount'); HealthCare.gov income page (federal taxable wages; 'Include most IRA and 401k withdrawals'; 'Include all unemployment compensation'). The statute text itself was not read for these points: the govinfo copy of 26 U.S.C. 36B is the 2024 edition and still shows the pre-2026 caps and the 2021-2025 rule. Severance counts as federal taxable wages per CL490. Added from the persona pass (CFP-2). Checker 2026-11-16: enhanced credits confirmed still lapsed; some states run their own premium help, so the block says 'no federal credit'.

new_claims.claim: Medicaid and CHIP accept applications any time of year; financial eligibility for Medicaid applicants is based on current monthly household income, and CHIP applies the same methodology
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 42 CFR 435.603(h)(1) ('must be based on current monthly household income and family size'), read on eCFR as of 2026-11-12; HealthCare.gov ('You can apply for Medicaid and CHIP any time of year'). HealthCare.gov also warns of a new monthly Medicaid work requirement in expansion states from 2027-01-01 and narrower immigrant eligibility; neither is in the block text. Added from the persona pass (ADV-4). Checker 2026-11-16: 42 CFR 457.315(a) read on eCFR as of 2026-11-12 ('the State must apply the financial methodologies set forth in paragraphs (b) through (i) of § 435.603 ... for CHIP').

new_claims.claim: A health FSA must make the full annual election available at any time during the coverage period and reimburses only expenses incurred during the period of coverage; HSA funds may pay COBRA premiums and health coverage premiums while receiving unemployment compensation
new_claims.source: IRS Publication 969 (2025), 'Distributions From an FSA' and HSA 'Insurance premiums'
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: IRS Pub. 969 (2025, dated 2026-02-11), FSA ('You must be able to receive the maximum amount of reimbursement ... at any time during the coverage period'; 'incurred during the period of coverage') and HSA premium exceptions (2) COBRA continuation coverage and (3) coverage while receiving unemployment compensation. Pub. 969 does not say an FSA balance is forfeited at separation, so the block does not say so. Added from the persona pass (CFP-3). The block now says 'on care you need'.

new_claims.claim: Each state runs its own unemployment insurance program and decides eligibility; file as soon as possible after becoming unemployed; 1099 income generally does not count toward a regular claim; many states treat severance (dismissal pay) as deductible income for the weeks it covers
new_claims.source: DOL 'How Do I File for Unemployment Insurance?'; Unemployment.gov (DOL); DOL ETA 'Comparison of State Unemployment Insurance Laws' (2023), ch. 5
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: DOL ('Each state administers a separate unemployment insurance program'; 'contact your state's unemployment insurance program as soon as possible after becoming unemployed'), Unemployment.gov ('the state UI agency will determine your eligibility'; 1099 income 'is not considered when assessing if you meet the work and wage requirements to establish a regular claim'), DOL Comparison of State UI Laws 2023, Nonmonetary chapter ('Many states consider wages in lieu of notice and dismissal payments to be deductible income'). DOL pages read via a fetch tool (dol.gov refuses curl); the comparison PDF read directly. This also supplies the source CL489 lacked for its state-administration clause. Added from the persona pass (ADV-3, CFP-6).

new_claims.claim: Federal student loan income-driven plans base the payment on income and family size, and in some cases it can be as low as $0; an unemployment deferment is available to borrowers receiving unemployment benefits or unable to find full-time work (not for loans made on or after July 1, 2027); payments must continue until a deferment is granted
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: studentaid.gov deferment page (read via Firecrawl; the page needs a browser): 'In some cases, your payment could be as low as $0 per month'; unemployment deferment 'up to three years'; 'won't be available for loans made on or after July 1, 2027'; 'You must continue making payments ... until you have been notified that your request for deferment has been granted.' The income-driven plans page itself and the new Repayment Assistance Plan's terms were not read; the block says only 'can be as low as'. Added from the persona pass (ADV-1, CFP-5).

new_claims.claim: SNAP is applied for in the state where you live, and benefits for an eligible household count from the date the application was submitted
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: USDA FNS SNAP eligibility page ('you must apply in the state in which you currently live'; 'you will receive benefits based on the date you submitted your application'). The page notes it is being updated for P.L. 119-21 changes to work requirements and non-citizen eligibility; neither is in the block text. Added from the persona pass (ADV-2).

new_claims.claim: A plan may pay out a small vested balance without the participant's consent; a mandatory distribution above a set amount goes to an IRA in the participant's name unless the participant elects otherwise, and smaller ones can be paid in cash; a distribution paid to you can be rolled over in whole or part within 60 days, making up any 20% withheld from other funds or that amount is taxable
new_claims.source: IRC §411(a)(11)(A), §401(a)(31)(B), §402(c)(3); IRS 'Rollovers of Retirement Plan and IRA Distributions'
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 26 U.S.C. 411(a)(11)(A) (consent required only if the present value exceeds $7,000), 401(a)(31)(B) (mandatory distributions in excess of $1,000 transferred to an IRA absent an election), govinfo 2024 edition; IRS rollovers page ('deposit all or a portion of it ... within 60 days'; 'you must use other funds to make up for the amount withheld'; worked example taxing the unrolled $2,000). Dollar thresholds deliberately not in the block text. Added from the persona pass (ADV-7, ADV-8a, CFP-8).

new_claims.claim: Be cautious if a financial professional suggests buying an annuity within a tax-deferred retirement plan or IRA; ask how the person recommending a rollover product is paid
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: Investor.gov ('Be cautious if a financial professional suggests you purchase an annuity within a tax-deferred retirement plan, such as a traditional 401(k) or traditional IRA'; 'The profit from this fee sometimes is also used to pay a commission to the financial professional who sold you the annuity'). 'Ask how they are paid' is the framework's inference from the commission sentence. Added from the persona pass (ADV-8b).

new_claims.claim: All of a person's IRAs are treated as one contract for taxing distributions, so a pre-tax IRA balance makes a later Roth conversion of nondeductible contributions partly taxable; money kept in an employer plan, old or new, is not in that total
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 26 U.S.C. 408(d)(2)(A) ('all individual retirement plans shall be treated as 1 contract'); Form 8606 instructions line 6 ('the total value of all your traditional IRAs as of December 31'). That an employer plan balance is excluded is a derivation from line 6 naming only IRAs, not a sentence read. Added from the persona pass (CFP-7).

new_claims.claim: Exercising a nonqualified stock option without a readily determinable value puts the gain (fair market value less the amount paid) into income at exercise; exercising an incentive stock option can create alternative minimum tax in that year
new_claims.source: IRS Topic No. 427, Stock options; IRC §56(b)(3)
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: IRS Topic 427 (page reviewed 2026-09-24): 'you may be subject to alternative minimum tax in the year you exercise an ISO'; for nonstatutory options without a readily determinable value 'you must include in income the fair market value of the stock received on exercise, less the amount paid'. 26 U.S.C. 56(b)(3) read for the ISO AMT adjustment. RSU/ESPP/deferred-compensation sentence is a pointer to plan documents, not a legal claim. Added from the persona pass (ADV-9, CFP-9).

new_claims.claim: An individual with excess elective deferrals allocates them and notifies the plan by March 1 of the following year, and the plan may distribute the excess by April 15; if not, it is taxed in the year contributed and again when distributed; excess Social Security tax withheld by two or more employers can generally be claimed as a credit on the income tax return
new_claims.source: IRC §402(g)(2)(A); IRS 'Consequences to a participant who makes excess deferrals'; IRS Topic No. 608
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 26 U.S.C. 402(g)(2)(A)(ii) ('not later than the 1st April 15 following the close of the taxable year, each such plan may distribute'); IRS consequences page ('taxed a second time when the deferrals are ultimately distributed'); IRS Topic 608 ('If you had more than one employer and too much Social Security tax ... withheld, you may be able to claim the excess as a credit'). Checker 2026-11-16: the March 1 allocation step (402(g)(2)(A)(i)) is now reflected as 'tell one plan early in the next year'. Added from the persona pass (CFP-10).

owner_decisions.what: Move the equity step ahead of the old-401k step, so the job-loss order becomes coverage, runway, equity, old-401k, withholding.
owner_decisions.why_owner: Reordering steps changes the module's shape. The event summary ('Health coverage and cash runway first; retirement-account decisions can wait for a calm week') and the equity step's own 'Check the grant documents now' both support the move; the old-401k step is 'Within 1-3 months' and is reversible, an expired option window is not.

draft.text_changes: None beyond those in this file; the equity block's new text already says to weigh exercise against runway.

owner_decisions.what: Two title edits: name Medicaid in the coverage title, and soften the old-401k title so it does not read as a ban.
owner_decisions.why_owner: The output format carries body text, not titles, and titles are the product's visible step names. Both changes follow accepted findings.

review.change: COBRA-drop sentence: 'you can switch only at open enrollment or when COBRA runs out' became 'you generally must wait for open enrollment unless COBRA runs out, an employer subsidy for it ends, or you have another life event'; 'after the first 60 days' anchored to 'since job coverage ended'; stopping payment named.
review.why: 'only' was wrong: HealthCare.gov and 45 CFR 155.420(e) also allow a switch when the employer stops contributing to COBRA and after another life event. 'The first 60 days' was ambiguous with the COBRA election window.

source.quote: You have to pay the full cost of COBRA coverage because your former employer stops contributing, or you lose a government subsidy (like COBRA premium assistance).

review.change: 'generally gets no credit / no help' became 'no federal credit / no federal help'.
review.why: The enhanced credits are confirmed still lapsed (IRS Q&A, updated 2026-02-19), but about a dozen states run their own premium help; the plain 'no help' overstated. Reworded to the federal credit the IRS page describes.

source.quote: In general, individuals and families may be eligible for the Premium Tax Credit if their household income for the year is at least 100 percent but no more than 400 percent of the federal poverty line

review.change: FSA sentence now says 'on care you need'.
review.why: A health FSA reimburses only qualified medical expenses incurred during the coverage period; the bare 'use any balance' could read as an instruction to spend for its own sake on a tight budget.

review.why: CFP-6 asked for net severance; the same block says severance is taxable wages with withholding, so the gross figure overstates runway.
